frontmatter.title: Use of the Two-State and Temporal Structure

children.value: The strategies in the previous chapter describe the response to a single displaced attack. This chapter asks which structure that response, and the placement in stable phases, reflects. If a participant represents two latent states, the direction of the other state is a more plausible destination of a change than the direction that is never a state, both for following a displaced attack and for placing single nets in stable phases. If the participant represents the temporal structure, a displaced attack late in an episode is more likely to be taken as a transition than one shortly after the last transition. The speed with which all nets arrive at the new direction after a transition shows how quickly the participant commits to a new state once the evidence accumulates.
Measures and models

All placements were expressed in the frame of the first color cue, with the allocation for the second cue rotated by the participant’s learned cue offset, and the shares of nets were counted within two positions (±22.5°) of a direction (
tambi_structure_measures.py
). The models are binomial generalized linear mixed models with logit link and the planned condition contrasts (
tambi_structure_use.R

); session half is coded −½ (first) and +½ (second). Random effects were reduced to random intercepts where the fit was singular. For the questionnaires, the standardized score and its interaction with the term of interest were added, with the Benjamini–Hochberg correction across the five questionnaires per term.
S1, direction of the oddball.

For each oddball, whether the placement at t+1 followed it (class followed, as in the previous chapter), as a function of condition, oddball type (pointing to the direction of the other latent state or to a direction that is never a state) and session half, with by-participant random intercepts and slopes for the oddball type.
S2, alternative directions in stable phases.

For each regular trial without an event in the three preceding trials, whether any net was at the direction of the other latent state and whether any net was at the direction that is never a state (both relative to the participant’s own placement centre on that trial), as a function of condition, direction, session half and position in the episode (per 10 trials), with by-participant random intercepts and slopes for the direction.
S3, temporal structure.

Whether the placement at t+1 followed an oddball, as a function of the number of trials since the last transition (S3a, per 10 trials), and whether it followed a transition, as a function of the length of the preceding episode (S3b), each with condition and session half.
S4, time to full commitment.

A discrete-time hazard model of the first placement after a transition at which the allocation was classified as followed (at least half of the nets at the new direction or a shift of at least 90°), for placements 1, 2, 3 and 4 or later, censored at the next oddball, the end of the episode or the tenth placement, with condition, session half and their interaction.
S5, change over the session.
Following at t+1, and a correct placement at t+2 (at the new direction after transitions, back at the t0 placement after oddballs), as a function of condition, event type and session half.
Direction of the oddball

Whether participants followed an oddball at t+1 did not depend on its direction on average (oddball type, 0.13 log-odds, p = .41), but the difference between the two oddball types changed over the session (oddball type × session half = 0.74, SE = 0.288, z = 2.56, p = .011) and depended on instruction (Full versus None and Partial × oddball type = 0.67, SE = 0.341, z = 1.98, p = .048). In the first half of the session, participants followed oddballs toward the other latent state about as often as oddballs toward the direction that is never a state, or less often (shares, None .25 and .25, Partial .17 and .30, Full .21 and .23). In the second half, they followed oddballs toward the other latent state more often in Full (.29 versus .11) and about as often in None (.23 versus .20) and Partial (.20 versus .19) (
Figure 1

). The three-way interaction with condition was not significant (Full versus None and Partial, 0.83, p = .21). No questionnaire was associated with following oddballs or with the difference between the oddball types (all q ≥ .34).

Alternative directions in stable phases

On regular trials in stable phases, at least one net was placed at an alternative direction on a small share of trials, more often in None and Partial than in Full (any net at the direction of the other latent state, None .11 and .09, Partial .09 and .10, Full .02 and .03, first and second half; at the direction that is never a state, None .08 and .06, Partial .07 and .07, Full .01 and .02). Nets at the direction of the other latent state were significantly more frequent than nets at the direction that is never a state (direction = 0.39 log-odds, SE = 0.119, z = 3.31, p < .001), in all conditions (condition × direction, both p ≥ .42). Nets at either alternative direction were significantly less frequent in Full than in None and Partial (planned contrast = −1.66, SE = 0.351, z = −4.74, p < .001) and became rarer the longer the episode had lasted (position in the episode = −0.26 per 10 trials, SE = 0.076, z = −3.42, p < .001). From the first to the second half of the session, they became more frequent in Full relative to None and Partial (Full versus None and Partial × session half = 0.57, SE = 0.217, z = 2.60, p = .009) and in Partial relative to None (0.27, SE = 0.129, z = 2.06, p = .039), without a change on average (0.11, p = .18). No questionnaire was associated with nets at alternative directions or with the difference between the two directions (all q ≥ .41).
Temporal structure

Participants followed an oddball at t+1 significantly more often the more trials had passed since the last transition (0.30 log-odds per 10 trials, SE = 0.145, z = 2.08, p = .038), and this dependence was significantly stronger in Full than in None and Partial (Full versus None and Partial × trials since the last transition = 0.97, SE = 0.336, z = 2.89, p = .004). Whether they followed a transition at t+1 did not depend on the length of the preceding episode (−0.003, p = .99), in any condition (both interactions p ≥ .67). No questionnaire was associated with the dependence on the trials since the last transition (all q ≥ .41). In the model of the transitions, higher STICSA state anxiety (−0.34 log-odds per SD, p = .020, q = .060) and BDI scores (−0.33, p = .024, q = .060) were associated with following transitions less often at t+1, as in the strategy analysis, without surviving the correction, independently of the length of the preceding episode (questionnaire × episode length, all p ≥ .08).
Time to full commitment after transitions

children.label: Time to full commitment after transitions

children.value: The share of transitions after which all or most nets were at the new direction by the first, second and fourth placement was .27, .52 and .67 in None, .28, .48 and .66 in Partial and .47, .72 and .83 in Full; after 24 % (None), 25 % (Partial) and 14 % (Full) of the transitions, this did not happen before the next oddball, the end of the episode or the tenth placement (
Figure 2

). In the discrete-time hazard model, the probability of committing at a given placement, among transitions without commitment so far, was significantly higher in Full than in None and Partial (planned contrast = 0.76 log-odds, SE = 0.247, z = 3.09, p = .002) and did not differ between Partial and None (0.04, p = .89). It was highest at the second placement (relative to the first, 0.34, p = .016) and lower from the fourth placement on (−0.48, p = .002), and it was significantly lower in the second half of the session than in the first (−0.29, SE = 0.113, z = −2.60, p = .009), in all conditions (condition × session half, both p ≥ .57). No questionnaire was associated with the hazard of commitment (all p ≥ .14, all q ≥ .44).

Change over the session

Across the session halves, the difference between transitions and oddballs in following at t+1 was significantly larger in Full than in None and Partial (Full versus None and Partial × event type = 1.07 log-odds, SE = 0.290, z = 3.69, p < .001) and did not change from the first to the second half (event type × session half, −0.06, p = .80; condition × event type × session half, both p ≥ .38). At t+2, the share of correct placements was significantly higher in Full (planned contrast = 1.22, SE = 0.187, z = 6.56, p < .001), and its difference between the events changed over the session (event type × session half = −0.57, SE = 0.218, z = −2.60, p = .009). From the first to the second half, correct placements at t+2 after transitions became less frequent (None .47 to .34, Partial .44 to .32, Full .70 to .64), and correct returns to the t0 placement after oddballs more frequent in None (.35 to .43), slightly less frequent in Partial (.45 to .41) and unchanged in Full (.67 to .67).

Higher STICSA state anxiety (event type × questionnaire = −0.30 log-odds per SD, SE = 0.118, z = −2.54, p = .011, q = .034), STICSA trait anxiety (−0.27, p = .022, q = .036) and BDI scores (−0.29, p = .014, q = .034) were associated with a smaller difference between transitions and oddballs in following at t+1, the trial-level counterpart of the lower selectivity in the strategy analysis. For IU, the difference between transitions and oddballs at t+1 increased from the first to the second half with higher scores (event type × session half × questionnaire = 0.52, p = .028, q = .14). No questionnaire was associated with correct placements at t+2 or with their change over the session (all q ≥ .50).
Summary

Participants in all conditions placed single nets in stable phases more often at the direction of the other latent state than at the direction that is never a state, and from the first to the second half of the session participants told the structure came to follow oddballs toward the other latent state more often than oddballs toward the direction that is never a state. Participants told the structure followed an oddball more readily the longer the episode had lasted, committed to the new direction after a transition at a higher rate, and placed fewer nets at alternative directions in stable phases. Over the session, the hazard of commitment after transitions decreased in all conditions, and correct placements at t+2 shifted from transitions toward oddballs. Of the questionnaire terms, those for the difference between transitions and oddballs on the first placement after the event were significant after correction. The terms for the measures of the two-state structure, of the dependence on the time since the last transition and of the time to full commitment were not significant individually, but had the same sign for all five questionnaires in three of the four measures. Higher scores went with a smaller preference for following oddballs toward the other latent state relative to the direction that is never a state (oddball type × questionnaire, −0.06 to −0.24 log-odds per SD), a weaker dependence of following oddballs on the trials since the last transition (−0.03 to −0.25) and a lower hazard of full commitment after transitions (−0.06 to −0.15), and, for four of the five questionnaires, with a slightly larger preference for the direction of the other latent state among the nets at alternative directions in stable phases (−0.02 to 0.11). Because the five questionnaires are correlated (Spearman ρ between .41 and .74), these signs are not independent observations.
